item.title: Linux Detection Engineering - Fileless Execution
item.description:
Linux fileless execution is not invisible: Elastic maps five memfd-based tradecraft patterns to concrete eBPF telemetry starting in Elastic Security 9.4.0, with detection rules and the open-source FENIX lab framework.
- memfd_create is the pivot point. The syscall creates an anonymous memory-backed fd with no path on disk, then the payload is written in and executed via /proc/self/fd/N. Elastic Defend 9.4.0 on kernel 5.10.16+ now records this as a process event with process.Ext.memfd.name and process.Ext.memfd.flags fields, making the full chain queryable: download, memfd_create, exec sequence visible in EQL without relying on procfs paths in child processes. Real-world examples include the malicious sympy-dev PyPI package and VoidLink paired with a rootkit that scanned for memfd-backed PIDs to hide.
- Five distinct execution classes each leave different artifacts: anonymous memfd-backed ELF exec (/proc/self/fd/N as execve path), interpreter one-liners where python3/perl/php calls memfd_create internally, fileless staging via curl/wget piped to an interpreter, deleted-file execution where /proc/PID/exe shows "path (deleted)" while the process runs on an open inode, and fileless LKM loading via finit_module on a memfd fd. Each class needs separate detection logic.
- LKM loading gets new visibility: init_module and finit_module calls now surface as load_module event actions on process events in 9.4.0.

item.title: ClickFix Moves into the Browser to Steal Cryptocurrency
item.description:
ClickFix evolves from OS command injection to in-browser JavaScript hijacking, targeting crypto traders with fake vulnerability lures and a persistent Google Sheets-hosted payload chain.
- The lure is social engineering aimed at would-be fraudsters: victims on Telegram, DarkForums, and paste sites were told a non-existent API flaw at crypto swap services would pay up to 38% more on deposits. They were instructed to paste JavaScript into Chrome's address bar, or from mid-April 2026, install Tampermonkey and add a malicious script. The appeal to targets who believed they were committing fraud is deliberate, suppressing victim reporting.
- Payload delivery abused the Google Visualization API to pull obfuscated code from a publicly published Google Sheets document. The request originated from the victim's own browser, blending into normal traffic. Payload cells were hidden by formatting text white on white. Talos recovered 21 second-stage payloads, rotated with fresh XOR keys and randomized variable names but functionally identical.
- The injected scripts acted as a full in-browser skimmer: monitoring page changes, replacing displayed deposit addresses, overriding the browser's fetch API to substitute attacker wallets before responses rendered, and replacing clipboard contents on copy. The Tampermonkey variant reloaded on every site visit for persistence.

item.title: Agents Gone Wild: An AI-Orchestrated Global Campaign Against PaperCut NG/MF
item.description:
A likely Russian-speaking actor used AI agents to exploit two PaperCut NG/MF CVEs, compromising 440 instances across 395 organizations in 48 countries, achieving domain admin in as little as five minutes after initial access.
- CVE-2026-81578 and CVE-2026-82078 are the two PaperCut vulnerabilities exploited. PaperCut runs as SYSTEM by default on Windows and is typically domain-joined, making it a direct path to Active Directory. The actor built a lab, validated RCE and credential harvesting, then launched at scale from 45.142.193[.]132, tracked by GreyNoise since July 2026.
- AI orchestration compressed the kill chain drastically: empty workspace to first victim RCE in under four hours, domain admin two hours later, then 11 organizations compromised in 26 seconds once the full campaign launched. OpenAI Codex and a DeepSeek model coordinated hundreds of agents alongside public offensive tooling.
- Three domain escalation paths observed: LSASS and registry secret harvesting into pass-the-hash; noPac (CVE-2021-42278/CVE-2021-42287) where unpatched; or direct Domain Admins group add if PaperCut ran as a DA service account. All paths ended with DCSync and a full NTDS.DIT exfil.
- Education sector in the US 🇺🇸 was heavily represented, consistent with PaperCut's customer base. Domain admin was confirmed at 12 organizations. Follow-on objectives remain unclear but prior PaperCut intrusions led to extortion.

item.title: CERT Polska alerts MikroTik RouterOS vulnerabilities actively being exploited in ‘MikroTrick’ attack chain
item.description:
MikroTik RouterOS hit by actively exploited two-flaw chain 'MikroTrick,' enabling unauthenticated full admin takeover of internet-exposed devices via SSH. Attacks confirmed since at least Sept. 2, 2026.
- CVE-2026-67276 (CVSS 9.2): SSH auth bypass via improper RSA public key comparison. An attacker knowing only a username and public modulus can craft a substitute key and log in without the private key, inheriting that account's privileges. CVE-2026-86060 (CVSS 9.2): crafted username triggers privilege escalation to full admin on SSH login. These two form the MikroTrick chain. CVE-2026-67277 (CVSS 8.8) adds kernel memory leakage and remote DoS via the bandwidth-test service.
- Observed attacker behavior: creation of a privileged account named 'ops,' failed logins under user '-2' followed by SSH-based user addition. Traffic originated from 82.192.72[.]4 and 103.102.31[.]18.
- Post-update, RouterOS scans config at startup and sets a 'Flagged' marker if it detects known compromise traces. Absence of that marker does NOT clear the device. Check logs for the compromise message and inspect for unknown users, scripts, scheduler tasks, proxies, and tunnels.
- Fixed in RouterOS 7.25beta3, 7.24.2, 7.23.4, and 6.49.21. If patching is blocked, immediately restrict SSH, WWW/WWW-SSL, and bandwidth-test to trusted management IPs only.

item.title: PoisonedRefresh: A Fileless Linux Rootkit That Injects PHP Web Shells Into F5 BIG-IP APM Server Memory
item.description:
PoisonedRefresh is a fileless Linux rootkit targeting F5 BIG-IP APM, injecting PHP web shells entirely into Apache process memory via CVE-2025-53521, an actively exploited unauthenticated RCE.
- CVE-2025-53521 is the initial access vector: an unauthenticated RCE in BIG-IP APM when an access policy is configured on a virtual server. Previously misclassified as a DoS issue, F5 confirmed RCE status. Shadowserver counted 795 exposed endpoints at disclosure. Patch and follow F5 compromise-assessment guidance before any other hardening.
- PoisonedRefresh (Sophos: Linux/Agnt-IC) is stage two. It intercepts __libc_start_main before Apache logging initializes, hooks apr_dso_load to wait for libphp, then patches mmap behavior inside libphp so Apache worker processes see a web shell prepended to legitimate BIG-IP APM webtop files (apm_css.php3, full_wt.php3, webtop_popup_css.php3). The on-disk files are never touched. SHA-256: 26bd5b0722d1dbab5db749a063c49bc8638653ac2addfead7a9cb3d6d57bccc9.
- The web shell triggers on the magic prefix BSOHAzPB in php://input, decrypts commands with key wSLjN1beuR, and responds HTTP 201 with Content-Type: text/css to blend into normal APM traffic. A UNIX socket at /run/bigtlog.pipe (token Kzwd6jM5) provides an interactive bash shell without opening any TCP port.
- Stage one hides inside a trojanized umount binary, infects /usr/sbin/httpd, and embeds in BIG-IP upgrade images for persistence across device updates.

item.title: CVE-2025-25249 Exploitation Delivers PivotC2, a FortiGate Post-Exploitation RAT
item.description:
CVE-2025-25249 actively exploited since July 2026: Russian-speaking crew drops PivotC2, a Node.js RAT purpose-built for FortiGate post-exploitation, hitting 178 confirmed devices from a 30,000-IP target list.
- CVE-2025-25249 (CVSS 9.8) is a heap-based buffer overflow in the FortiOS/FortiSwitchManager cw_acd daemon, reachable unauthenticated over UDP 5246. The exploit binary fortirun.bin (SHA256: 2d338f...) fingerprints firmware via CAPWAP discovery, leaks live memory pointers to defeat ASLR, groans the heap with crafted Add Station messages, then corrupts a doubly-linked free list to gain write-what-where and pivot execution into Node.js, which ships natively with FortiOS, no dropper needed.
- PivotC2 (v0.2.3, AI-assisted) lands at /tmp/.i.js after a Base64+XOR (key: pivot) stager fetches it from hxxps://146.103.99[.]177:8443/0c5b76709523. It beacons out over a single TLS socket, multiplexing shells, file ops, SOCKS5/HTTP tunneling, port forwarding, and CIDR scanning. Auto-mode autonomously harvests /data/config/sys_global.conf.gz, /data/config/sys_vd_root+root.conf.gz, and /data/etc/fsv_sync.dat, then decrypts ENC credentials (AES-256-CBC or AES-128-GCM) yielding VPN PSKs, SSL-VPN creds, LDAP bind secrets, and admin accounts.

item.title: Vwork: Weaponized Open-source Software as an Addon for Gigabud
item.description:
GoldFactory's Gigabud RAT now deploys Vwork, a weaponized fork of open-source Android app Shelter, to clone banking apps into a hidden work profile and bypass fraud detection across 11+ countries.
- Vwork (package name net.yy.vwork) is a repackaged version of the legitimate Shelter cloning app. GoldFactory stripped its user-facing controls, translated the UI to Chinese 🇨🇳, hid its launcher icon (T1628.001), and exposed cloning functions as an API. Three new Gigabud C2 commands drive it: initVwa, cloneApp, and uploadCloneApps. Cloned packages are prefixed vwa- in C2 traffic, a hunt-ready pattern.
- The evasion logic is deliberate. Gigabud infects the personal profile, triggers a fraud detection alert with no transaction loss, then Vwork provisions a clean work profile and clones the target banking app there (T1629, T1630). The bank sees a transaction from what looks like a new device with no malware signal. The fraud bypasses controls that already fired.
- Both Gigabud and Vwork are packed with dpt-shell (T1406.002). Gigabud uses HTTPS on port 9000 and WebSocket on port 8888 for RTMP video streaming (T1437.001, T1509). C2 payload is AES-ECB encrypted. Full SHA-256 hashes for 7 Gigabud samples, 1 Vwork sample, and 1 modified banking APK are in the report.
- Confirmed on Indonesian 🇮🇩 devices Feb-Jul 2026: 1,469 compromised devices, ~$961K in observed losses.

item.title: THost9 Android RAT Pairs Packed Loader With ADB Worm
item.description:
THost9 Android RAT combines a packed loader with an ADB worm that auto-spreads across exposed devices, active in incidents from October 2024 through mid-2026.
Key findings:
- The loader hides its second-stage payload (tc9.dex) inside an APK asset, decoded with single-byte XOR then gzip-decompressed and loaded dynamically. It starts a foreground service, scrubs itself from Android's Recents view, and requests accessibility service control where protected settings are already granted.
- The second stage adds shell execution, file transfers, tunneling, reverse-shell, and downloadable modules. One build exposed an unauthenticated local controller socket. A newer build exits on Frida detection, a direct anti-analysis countermeasure targeting researchers.
- The ADB worm is the standout: it discovers exposed ADB services via local service-discovery or operator targets, expands a single address to a 65,025-host sweep using 50 concurrent workers, authenticates with pre-loaded ADB key material, retrieves the installer, and runs it. On privileged sessions it can modify ADB settings and drop itself into a system directory.
- Incident records link THost9 and predecessor THost4 to compromised Android phones and Redroid containers with public ADB exposure, spanning October 2024 to a July 2026 remediation that rebounded a Redroid deployment to localhost after infection.

item.title: Improper OTP Implementation to Full Account Takeover
item.description:
An OTP endpoint returned the one-time code in its own HTTP response body, collapsing MFA to zero protection and enabling full admin account takeover with no phishing or SIM-swap required. CVSS 3.1: 9.8.
Key findings:
- Account enumeration started in the production JavaScript bundle at /static/js/main.[hash].js, which exposed four internal email addresses. A POST to /Mail/Validation_Email confirmed valid accounts and returned each user's internal idPersonnal in plaintext, handing a definitive yes/no plus an internal record ID to any unauthenticated caller.
- POST to /Mail/Insert_Rel_EmailCode returned the full OTP in the response body: {"email":"admin.user@targetapp.example[.]com","code":"085327","idPersonnal":5741}. The endpoint's job was to email the code, not echo it to the caller. No inbox access was needed.
- The OTP was not single-use, had no enforced expiry, and was not bound to the session or device that requested it. Code 085327 was replayed directly as the second factor, producing an authenticated admin session. OWASP API2:2023 / A07:2021.
- The full chain (enumeration, OTP leak, replay) used only the platform's public API with a generic bearer token and is trivially scriptable end-to-end.
During pen tests and IR, hit every OTP-send endpoint with a proxy and read the raw response: if the code appears anywhere outside the out-of-band channel, MFA is theater. Also grep production JS bundles for hardcoded emails and internal IDs before they ship.

item.title: Token Analysis and Tracking System (TATS)
item.description:
TATS is a new open-source tool for live OAuth token tracking in Microsoft cloud environments, and it already uncovered two CAP gaps defenders need to understand.
Key findings:
- TATS (github.com/IceMoonHSV/TATS) collects and decodes OAuth tokens via Burp import, Chrome DevTools Protocol, or mitmproxy, storing them in a database with a web GUI. It visualizes exchanges as Mermaid graphs and sequence diagrams, tracks refresh token chains, and flags FOCI and brokered client ID (BroCI) behavior specific to Microsoft's OAuth deviations.
- Audience mismatch: tokens issued with management.core.windows[.]net as the aud claim were accepted by management.azure[.]com and portal.azure[.]com, meaning Microsoft is not strictly enforcing audience binding as OAuth spec requires.
- Pre-MFA token issuance: after username and password entry, access and refresh tokens were issued before the MFA prompt appeared. The amr claim confirmed MFA was absent. While the portal itself enforced MFA, those tokens could be brokered to nested apps like Key Vault if no explicit Conditional Access Policy (CAP) covered them.
- The CAP gap is the real risk: relying solely on MFA enforcement at the admin portal level leaves nested applications exposed to token brokering abuse if they lack their own CAP.
Defenders: audit your CAPs to confirm MFA is required at the resource level, not just the portal.

item.title: The Job Offer Has Claws: Mirage Kitten Deploys NodeRabbit and PollCat
item.description:
Iranian 🇮🇷 group Mirage Kitten targets software engineers with trojanized coding challenges, deploying two new cross-platform RATs: NodeRabbit and PollCat, hitting fintech, aviation, and aerospace sectors across the Middle East and Africa.
Key findings:

A trojanized Express/React/Vite app called TaskFlow hid a malicious npm package, colorized_terminal v2.1.0, bundled directly in node_modules to avoid registry detection. Importing it silently launched NodeRabbit from node_modules/.cache/.320697f1/index.js.
- NodeRabbit (3 variants) is a Node.js RAT with AES-256-GCM encrypted C2 over Azure infrastructure. Variant 3 expands to 23 commands including Outlook OST/PST harvesting, VS Code extension persistence masquerading as "GitHub Copilot Helper", and Git hook injection via .git/hooks/post-merge and post-checkout to retrigger execution on normal developer Git activity.
- PollCat starts C2 registration before OTP authentication completes, persists via scheduled tasks (Windows), cron (Linux), or LaunchAgent (macOS), and fingerprints 24 security vendors including CrowdStrike, SentinelOne, and Fortinet via SYSTEM_CHECK. Its EVAL_JS command executes arbitrary attacker-supplied JavaScript with full Node.js module access.

item.title: CVE-2026-75650: Adobe Patches Actively Exploited Magento Zero-Day Used to Deploy Backdoors
item.description:
CVE-2026-75650, CVSS 10.0 zero-day in Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source, is actively exploited. Unauthenticated RCE via template injection deployed Rust backdoors and PHP web shells before Adobe's Sept 7 patch.
Key findings:
- StyleSmuggler (CWE-1336) poisons a server-accessible file (app log or var/report/) with attacker PHP, then triggers Magento's template engine through the Payment Transaction Failed Reminder email flow to include and execute it. No account, no user interaction required. Full August 2026 security updates offered zero protection.
- Two distinct post-exploitation paths confirmed: a Rust-based Linux implant masquerading as [kworker/u:8:0], fc-cache, or chronyd, persisting via cron and UDP/123 NTP-like traffic; and a PHP web shell dropped under pub/media/catalog/product/cache/ returning 404 until triggered with X-Cache-Token header. C2 infrastructure resolved to 185.157.160[.]251.
- First exploitation confirmed Sept 4 at 22:20 UTC, three days before Adobe bulletin APSB26-146 and hotfix VULN-39341 shipped. Any internet-facing store in that window must be treated as potentially compromised, not just unpatched.
- Malware survived file deletion by relocating outside the webroot, re-establishing cron persistence, and continuing execution. Deleting the web shell is not remediation.
Apply VULN-39341 and rotate Commerce encryption keys now.

item.title: ClickFix moves into the browser: Cryptocurrency theft with Google-hosted C2
item.description:
ClickFix evolves into the browser: actors abuse Google Visualization API as C2 to steal cryptocurrency by hijacking fetch calls, clipboard, and deposit addresses inside live trading sessions.
Key findings:

The social engineering hook is a fake "API Logic Flaw" vulnerability report promising 25-38% bonus payouts, aimed squarely at would-be fraudsters.
- C2 is a publicly published Google Sheets document queried via the unauthenticated Visualization API at docs.google[.]com/spreadsheets/d/[id]/gviz/tq. The first-stage loader, pasted by the victim into Chrome's address bar as javascript: or into Tampermonkey, pulls two obfuscated cells from the sheet, reconstructs a payload in memory, and injects it into the live page. Tampermonkey install also provides cross-session persistence.
- The second-stage skimmer overrides the browser's fetch API to swap legitimate wallet addresses in JSON responses, hijacks clipboard copy events, and uses MutationObserver to re-apply replacements after DOM updates. 49 BTC addresses were embedded; 24 received funds totaling 0.159 BTC, with proceeds routed through 3,000+ additional addresses consistent with mixing.

item.title: CVE-2026-86206, CVE-2026-86207: N-able N-central Authentication Bypass (FIXED)
item.description:
Two chained flaws in N-able N-central let an unauthenticated remote attacker bypass auth and create a System Administrator account. Patch to version 2026.3.1.13 immediately.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-86206 (CVSS 6.9) is a path-parsing and header-spoofing bypass. A crafted URI like /dms;/services/ServerUI fools Envoy into routing the request while Jetty strips the semicolon and dispatches to the protected SOAP servlet. Simultaneously, a Forwarded header with for="127.0.0.\1" causes Jetty to resolve the address as 127.0.0.1, while N-central's own LocalHostUtils parser sees an invalid value and fails open, granting local trust to a remote caller.
- CVE-2026-86207 (CVSS 7.7) is an auth bypass in UserTwoFactorLogin. Built-in accounts (User ID 1 N-able Administrator, 50 Product Administrator, 51 N-able Support) have no legacy 2FA profile, so calling User.TwoFactorLogin with a dummy password throws an exception. The session-user binding set before the auth attempt is never cleaned up, leaving a fully authenticated SOAP session without valid credentials.
- Chained, these give a remote unauthenticated attacker a privileged SOAP session they can use to create a new attacker-controlled System Administrator account via the ServerUI2 endpoint. All N-central versions before 2026.3.1.13 are vulnerable.
On-premise N-central operators: apply N-central 2026.3 Hotfix 3 (2026.3.1.13) out-of-band now.

item.title: CVE-2026-67276: MikroTik RouterOS SSH Zero-Day Exploited in Router Takeover Attacks
item.description:
CVE-2026-67276 (CVSS 9.2): MikroTik RouterOS SSH auth-bypass was exploited as a zero-day before patches shipped, enabling full router takeover when chained with CVE-2026-86060.
Active exploitation confirmed:
- CVE-2026-67276 (CWE-347) lets an attacker authenticate via SSH as any RouterOS user without possessing the private key. RouterOS only partially validated the RSA public key modulus, so a crafted key passes verification. Knowing a valid username and the target account's public modulus is enough. Chained with CVE-2026-86060, a privilege-escalation bug triggered by SSH usernames beginning with a prohibited character, unauthenticated attackers gain full administrative control. CERT Polska named this two-stage chain MikroTrick. Exploitation confirmed from 82.192.72[.]4 and 103.102.31[.]18. Observed post-compromise artifact: a privileged account named ops.
- Zero-day window is real. Evidence places exploitation at September 2, 2026, one day before MikroTik published fixes on September 3. Patch any device with public SSH exposure and treat it as potentially compromised, not just unpatched.
- Log indicators to hunt now: "login failure for user -2 via ssh" and "user added by ssh:-2@IP". The string -2 is not a valid RouterOS username and maps directly to the privilege-manipulation stage.
Patch to RouterOS 7.24.2, 7.23.5, or 6.49.21. Run /system/device-mode/print and check for Flagged status.

item.title: Dissecting a PHP web server rootkit
item.description:
A fileless PHP web shell implant targeting F5 BIG-IP APM systems uses custom ELF loading, APR function hooking, and in-memory mmap patching to deliver attacker access with zero on-disk web shell artifacts.
Key findings:
- CVE-2025-53521 is the initial access vector: an unauthenticated RCE in BIG-IP APM when an access policy is configured on a virtual server. The second-stage payload (SHA256: 26bd5b0722d1dbab5db749a063c49bc8638653ac2addfead7a9cb3d6d57bccc9, detected as Linux/Agnt-IC) is deployed by a first-stage installer that infects /usr/sbin/httpd and survives BIG-IP upgrade images by targeting /mnt/tm_install workflows.
- Execution begins before Apache's main() by hijacking __libc_start_main via a custom ELF loader that reads /proc/self/exe, manually maps an embedded ELF, and installs a wrapper, giving the implant full API resolution before any application thread starts. RC4 with key TrswBWIl90Z5e38n hides all operational strings at rest.
- The web shell never touches disk. The implant hooks apr_dso_load to detect libphp loading, then patches open, mmap, and fxstat inside libphp to intercept PHP's file reads of apm_css.php3, full_wt.php3, and webtop_popup_css.php3. At mmap time it prepends the embedded PHP payload in memory only. The shell checks for magic prefix BSOHAzPB, decrypts with key wSLjN1beuR, evals, and returns HTTP 201 with Content-Type: text/css to blend in.

item.title: Digital Forensics: Fixing a Corrupted Disk After File Exfiltration
item.description:
Corrupted MBR used to obstruct investigation into insider data exfiltration. NTFS artifacts including $MFT and $UsnJrnl expose the full attack chain despite deliberate anti-forensic wiping.
Key findings:
- The MBR's final two bytes (boot signature 0x55 0xAA) were overwritten to prevent tools like Autopsy and FTK Imager from reading the image. Repair requires a hex editor such as HxD: overwrite, never delete, those bytes to restore the signature before any further analysis.
- After repair, export and parse MFT with MFTECmd.exe (Eric Zimmerman's EZTools): MFTECmd.exe -f ..\Evidence$MFT --csv ..\Evidence\ --csvf MFT.csv. Even deleted file records survive here, revealing Excel sheets, PDFs, and zip archives flagged as sensitive corporate data.
- $UsnJrnl (J) logged the full exfiltration sequence: a folder named "data Exfil" was created, files were appended to "New Compressed (zipped) Folder.zip", then renamed and deleted. Parse J with MFTECmd, open in Timeline Explorer, and filter Update Reason to FileDelete.
- DiskWipe.exe was found on the second partition. To confirm execution and tie actions to a user, extend the investigation into Prefetch, Shellbags, registry, and NTUSER.DAT.
Always hash-verify the forensic image before touching it, then work only on a verified copy. MFT and $UsnJrnl together reconstruct what wipers try to erase.

item.title: PEEP: A Browser RAT Posing as a Chrome Extension
item.description:
PEEP, a RedExt-derived browser RAT disguised as "Smart Bookmarks," converts Chrome and Edge into persistent backdoors with host-level command execution, session theft, and file access, all over plaintext HTTP.
Key findings:
- PEEP is a post-exploitation toolkit requiring prior admin or code execution access. Its PowerShell installers (install_silent.ps1, patch_secure_prefs.ps1) forge Chromium's Secure Preferences HMAC-SHA256 integrity values (protection.macs and super_mac) so the sideloaded extension passes the browser's own integrity check and silently re-enables at every launch (T1553). Four layered persistence mechanisms, Secure Preferences forgery, enterprise ExtensionInstallForcelist policy, external sideloading, and a ScriptCache "Ghost Anchor" fallback, mean no single cleanup action removes all of it.
- The native-messaging host com.peep.lab (nm_host.exe, a 37.7 MB unsigned Node.js pkg binary) bridges the browser sandbox to the OS, supporting NM_SHELL (cmd/PowerShell/bash), filesystem read/write/delete, process listing, and service enumeration. The agent beacons every 30 seconds over plaintext HTTP to 206.237.30[.]232 (AS55933, Cloudie, Hong Kong) with X-PEEP-Agent-Key and X-PEEP-Agent-Id headers, auto-exfiltrating cookies, history, and open tabs to /api/exfil.

item.title: Attacking and Defending SCOM: Management Server Relay and Obtaining Run As Credentials
item.description:
Default SCOM deployments hand attackers a path from standard domain user to code execution on every monitored host, including domain controllers, via NTLM relay and DPAPI credential dumping.
Key findings:
- The relay attack targets the MSOMSdkSvc/ SPN sitting on the Management Server computer account by default. Using PetitPotam to coerce authentication and impacket-ntlmrelayx to relay it, an attacker inserts their SID into the AzMan_Role_SIDMember table in the OperationsManager database, granting Operations Console access from a standard domain account. SCOMHunter automates the enumeration and relay query.
- Once in the Operations Console, attackers create Agent Tasks targeting any monitored host, including domain controllers, running as SYSTEM. A single task like "cmd.exe /c net group Domain Admins domainuser /add /domain" completes the escalation.

item.title: How Attackers Learn Your Network Before They Attack It
item.description:

- bro-simple-scan watches Zeek connection history strings, S (SYN with no response) and Sr (SYN plus RST), counting unique victim/port pairs per source. At 25 failures it fires one of three notices: Scan::Address_Scan (one source, many hosts), Scan::Port_Scan (one source, one host, many ports), or Scan::Random_Scan (scattered pattern). Darknet integration via bro-is-darknet drops the threshold to 10 when a source touches unused address space, and a separate knock-knock rule fires at 20 unique hosts on a single port (3 if darknet).
- The structural blind spot is slow and distributed scanning. State ages out after 15 minutes by default, so a scanner pacing below two probes per half hour never accumulates enough failures. Split across 50 sources, no single source trips a per-source threshold even when the aggregate pattern is obvious.
- Profile-based detection is the upgrade path. A SYN to a port no host in your network legitimately serves is high-confidence at count one. Zeek already logs every connection; building a baseline of which hosts serve which ports, and who talks to whom, inverts the detection question from "has this source failed enough?" to "does this connection make sense?"

item.title: Attackers Actively Exploiting Critical Vulnerability in Elementor Pro Plugin
item.description:
CVE-2026-32475 (CVSS 9.8) in Elementor Pro is actively exploited, letting unauthenticated attackers upload PHP webshells and take over any WordPress site running the vulnerable plugin across 6 million active installs.

item.title: Gaming the system: how a Chinese-speaking actor turned Brazilian government sites into an SEO weapon

item.title: Android App RCE via Dynamic Code Loading
item.description:
Android document viewer app achieves RCE by chaining a path traversal in URI handling with dynamic native library loading, letting an attacker write and execute arbitrary code inside the app's sandbox.
Key findings:
- The vulnerable app's handleIntent() passes an attacker-controlled HTTP/HTTPS URI to copyFileFromUri(), which calls Uri.getLastPathSegment() without decoding percent-encoded characters. Supplying a URL like hxxps://192.168.x[.]x/..%2F..%2F..%2F..%2Fdata%2Fdata%2Fcom.mobilehackinglab.documentviewer%2Ffiles%2Fnative-libraries%2Fx86_64%2Flibdocviewer_pro.so causes the traversal to land outside the Downloads folder and write directly into the app's private files/ directory (T1083, T1105).
- loadProLibrary() unconditionally calls System.load() on files/native-libraries/ABI/libdocviewer_pro.so at every launch. An attacker plants a malicious .so compiled with ndk-build; on next app open, the library executes with the app's UID.
- The attack is delivered entirely via a crafted deep-link intent (scheme: file/http/https, mimeType: PDF), requiring no user permissions beyond what the app already holds.
Takeaway: When reviewing Android apps, flag any combination of getLastPathSegment() feeding a file write path and System.load() referencing that same path. Check AndroidManifest.xml for exported Activities accepting deep links, then trace URI handling through to any file-write or library-load call. Full exploit chain is documented in the write-up.
